title: Siblings, friends, family: how to lend money
subtitle: Lending to loved ones
openingQuestion: Your younger brother asks to borrow 200 million VND to open a coffee shop, promising to repay in 2 years, but only verbally, with no paperwork because 'we're family, writing it down would make things awkward.' Which approach is considered reasonable and protects both sides best?
openingOptions: Flatly refuse this loan request, since as a matter of principle you should never lend any amount of money to a family member
Lend the money right away exactly as verbally promised, since he's family and asking for paperwork would be seen as a lack of mutual trust
Lend him your entire retirement savings, placing absolute trust in your younger brother
Still lend the money, but draw up a loan document stating the amount and repayment schedule
explanation: Lending between relatives and friends is a common cause of damaged relationships - not because of a lack of trust, but because a lack of clarity leads to misunderstanding when the two sides remember things differently. Drafting a simple loan document (even just a few lines, signed by both sides) isn't a sign of suspicion - it's a way of protecting the RELATIONSHIP from later disputes ('I never said that,' 'I forget which month you promised to repay'). At the same time, only lend an amount you can ACCEPT LOSING entirely, never touching your emergency fund or retirement money.

realWorldExample.company: A survey of family disputes in Vietnam
realWorldExample.description: Many cases shared on legal advice and personal finance forums in Vietnam show that disputes over lending between relatives and friends usually center on the lack of clear paperwork - leading to disagreement over the amount borrowed, how much has been repaid, and what interest rate, if any, was verbally agreed. Some serious cases end up in civil court, but the lack of written evidence makes resolution extremely difficult, drags on for years, and permanently damages family relationships.

quiz.question: Why draft a loan document even when lending to relatives or friends?
options: Because having paperwork guarantees you'll definitely get the full amount back
Because clear paperwork avoids misunderstanding and protects the relationship
Because the law requires every personal loan to be in writing
Because a loan document exempts the loan from personal income tax
quiz.explanation: Paperwork isn't about showing distrust - it's so both sides share the same 'truth' about the agreement, avoiding later disputes caused by differing memories or misunderstandings.

quiz.question: What's the key principle for deciding how much to lend a relative?
options: Prefer withdrawing from your emergency fund, since that's idle money
Lend up to 50% of your current savings account balance
Only lend an amount you can accept losing entirely
Lend any amount at all, as long as there's full paperwork
quiz.explanation: Lending to relatives always carries the risk of never being repaid, even with paperwork. The safe principle is to only lend within what you can accept losing without threatening your own financial safety net.

quiz.question: What's the main reason lending within a family damages relationships?
options: Family borrowers almost never intend to repay in the first place
The lender always charges a much higher interest rate than a commercial bank
The law doesn't recognize loans made between family members
A lack of clarity from the start about amount, term, and repayment leads to misunderstanding
quiz.explanation: Most breakdowns don't come from bad intent - they come from both sides remembering the same agreement differently. Writing it down feels cold toward a relative, but it's exactly what protects the relationship.

quiz.question: What's the safest way to lend money to a relative?
options: Only lend an amount you're willing to accept losing without resentment
Require the borrower to pledge an asset worth more than the loan
Lend your entire savings so the relative can resolve their problem completely
Only lend if the relative agrees to pay a higher rate than a bank loan
quiz.explanation: If losing that amount still lets you sleep at night and still lets you face each other normally, the relationship survives regardless of the outcome. If not, say no - refusing once is far easier than chasing a debt for years.

quiz.question: What details should be written down when lending to a relative?
options: Just the amount is enough - the rest can stay flexible depending on the situation
The amount, the term, the repayment method, and what happens if payment is late
The borrower's entire income and assets, as a basis for assessment
Nothing at all, since paperwork destroys trust between both sides
quiz.explanation: Those four items eliminate nearly every source of misunderstanding. The hardest one is the last - stating upfront what happens if payment is late - but that's exactly the moment the relationship gets tested.

quiz.question: How does guaranteeing a relative's bank loan differ from lending directly?
options: Guaranteeing creates no legal obligation for the person who signs as guarantor
You're only responsible for the interest while the bank recovers the principal itself
You're liable for the full amount if the borrower defaults, even if you never handed over any money
The bank pays you a guarantee fee, making this a beneficial transaction for you
quiz.explanation: Signing as a guarantor means taking on debt without receiving any money. It also eats into your own credit limit, which can block your own home loan years later - a consequence almost nobody thinks about at the time of signing.

keyTakeaways: Drafting a clear loan document (amount, interest if any, repayment schedule, both signatures) protects the relationship - it isn't a sign of distrust
Only lend an amount you can accept losing entirely - never touch your emergency fund or retirement money
Agree clearly upfront on whether interest is charged, to avoid vagueness leading to misunderstanding
If unsure whether to lend, ask yourself: 'If I lost this money, would the relationship still be intact?'

practicePrompt.question: A friend asks to borrow 100 million VND to pay off high-interest credit card debt, promising to repay in 6 months. You have 300 million in savings, but that's nearly your entire emergency fund. What's the sensible way to handle this?
options: Only lend an amount you can accept losing entirely, without touching your emergency fund
Lend the full 100 million right away, since friendship matters more than any personal financial risk that could arise
Refuse every borrowing request from friends entirely, since this is always the wrong financial decision in every case
Lend the entire 300 million in savings to show absolute trust, regardless of whether it's your emergency fund or not
practicePrompt.explanation: The core principle is to only lend an amount you can accept losing entirely, without touching your emergency fund - protecting your own financial safety before helping someone else.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.

application.title: Draft it now
application.message: If you currently have a loan with a relative with no paperwork, write a few lines right now stating the amount, the date, the repayment schedule, and get both signatures.
application.secondary: A few minutes today can prevent a major argument later.

sections.text: 'Clear about money, decisive about affection' - this old Vietnamese saying is truer than ever when it comes to lending between relatives and friends. Plenty of good relationships have fractured not because of a large sum, but because of vagueness in the original agreement.

Lending between people who know each other differs from a bank loan in one important way: there's no neutral third party to settle a dispute, and emotional pressure makes both chasing a debt and refusing to lend far harder. That's exactly why setting clear ground rules upfront matters more, not less, than it does with a bank loan.
Three principles before deciding to lend

items: Only lend an amount you can accept NEVER getting back - this is the most important psychological test before deciding
Never draw from your own emergency fund or retirement money to lend to someone else
Discuss the borrower's actual ability to repay honestly, not just relying on affection or a promise
If it feels uncomfortable to refuse, you can propose a smaller amount instead of the full sum requested

sections.text: Why paperwork isn't a lack of trust

Many people hesitate to suggest a loan document for fear of being seen as 'not trusting family.' But in reality, simple paperwork just records exactly what both sides agreed to - preventing a situation where, over time, each side remembers the amount, the interest, or the deadline differently. A few lines stating the loan date, the amount, whether interest applies, the expected repayment schedule, and both signatures can prevent a great deal of unnecessary conflict later.

sections.title: Elements a family loan agreement should include

concepts.def: Write it in both numerals and words to avoid confusion
State clearly whether interest applies and at what %/year
Lump sum or installments, and the final deadline
Both sides sign, and it can be photographed and kept as evidence

lines: Lending between relatives isn't wrong - what matters is making things clear from the start, to protect both the money and the relationship.
A simple, transparent piece of paper today can save a relationship many years from now.
